o:
A digitorial number equals the sum of the factorials of its digits (e.g., 145 = 1!+4!+5!). We ask whether any rotation-free rearrangement of n's digits is digitorial. Since n ≤ 1e9 has at most 10 digits, brute-forcing permutations is conceivable but expensive (up to 10! arrangements); the elegant route uses the mathematical fact that the only base-10 factorions are 1, 2, 145, and 40585, so we merely compare digit multisets against these four.

Example 1: digits of 145 match 145 itself → true. Example 2: digits {1,0} match none of the four (and '01' is invalid anyway) → false.
k: The only digitorial numbers in base 10 are 1, 2, 145, 40585, so the answer reduces to a digit-multiset comparison.

a.i: Generate all distinct permutations of the digits, reject those with a leading zero, and test the factorial-sum condition. With ≤ 10 digits this is at most ~3.6M candidates — borderline but workable in fast languages, and it needs no mathematical knowledge.
s: Recursively generate distinct permutations of the digit multiset (skip repeats and leading zeros).
For each candidate, verify the digit-factorial sum equals the number.

c.python:
from itertools import permutations
class Solution:
    def isDigitorialPermutation(self, n):
        fact = [1]*10
        for i in range(1, 10): fact[i] = fact[i-1]*i
        digs = str(n)
        seen = set()
        for p in set(permutations(digs)):
            if p in seen or p[0] == '0': continue
            seen.add(p)
            num = int(''.join(p))
            if num == sum(fact[int(d)] for d in p):
                return True
        return False

a.t: O(d! · d) for d digits — up to ~3.6M permutations of 10 digits

a.i: It is a classical result that 1, 2, 145, and 40585 are the only numbers equal to the sum of their digits' factorials in base 10 (any such number has at most 7 digits since 8·9! + ... bounds the growth). Therefore n has a valid digitorial permutation iff its digit multiset equals that of one of these four numbers.
s: For each, compare sorted digit strings with sorted digits of n.
a.t: O(d log d) — sorting a ≤10-digit string four times

w: Lead with the whitelist approach and justify it (any factorion has at most 7 digits because 7·9! = 2540160 caps the sum for 8-digit numbers, and exhaustive search over that tiny range yields the four values). If challenged on the fact, fall back to Approach 1. Pitfall: forgetting that permutations starting with '0' are invalid — the whitelist sidesteps this automatically since none of the four numbers contains a 0.
